claims.text: Housing: the campaign's plan aims to add 40,000 owner-occupied homes Coloradans can afford, cutting the existing shortfall of such homes in half, with faster permitting, lower fees on homes under $600,000, down payment help, renter protections, and oversight of out-of-state investors and corporate landlords.
claims.sourceTitle: Campaign site: Affordable Homes and Communities

claims.text: Health care: the campaign's 'Healthy Colorado Plan' emphasizes prevention and primary care, more affordable insurance options, cheaper prescriptions, protections against surprise bills and medical debt, and a task force to shield care from federal cuts.

Public safety: the campaign says he would support police hiring and training, sign and defend gun safety laws, send trained co-responders to addiction and mental health crises, tie bail decisions to public safety risk rather than finances, and create a Governor's Office of Safe Communities.

The campaign's biography page says he is Colorado's Attorney General, clerked for U.S. Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, worked at the U.S. Department of Justice and the White House in the Clinton and Obama administrations, and chaired Governor Ritter's Innovation Council.

The campaign's home page lists these priorities: government accountability and transparency (ending waste and corruption); housing and cost of living; jobs, taxes and economic growth (cutting taxes); and law, order and public safety (backing law enforcement and putting victims first). Faith, freedom and nature appear as further headings with little detail on the page read.

The campaign's home page describes him as a husband, father and community servant who has overcome personal adversity, and says he has spent decades on front-line work supporting veterans, rescuing vulnerable people and building programs. It lists no prior elected office.

The campaign's biography page lists these priorities: lowering health care and prescription drug costs; reducing gun violence; protecting Colorado's public lands while addressing climate change; and working across party lines.

The campaign's biography page says he was elected Mayor of Denver and that he began as a geologist before opening Colorado's first brewpub and starting other small businesses. It says he ran for governor in 2010 and credits that work with results on job creation, climate and gun safety laws, and Medicaid expansion, but it does not state his terms or dates.

The campaign's issues page says he supports lower federal taxes, fewer regulations and more domestic energy production; more funding for law enforcement and an end to programs that release violent offenders early; and, on immigration, describes about 1.2 million people admitted legally each year after screening and says immigrants should be self-reliant and assimilate. For agriculture it favors fewer regulatory burdens and market-based solutions over expanded government programs.
The campaign's home page describes a career as an aerospace engineer and leading a Colorado software company, and says he was elected to the Colorado House in 2018 and the Colorado Senate in 2022.

The Colorado General Assembly's member page lists him as a Republican state senator for District 4 with assignments to the Joint Technology, Local Government & Housing, and Transportation & Energy committees. The page read did not state service dates.
claims.sourceTitle: Colorado General Assembly: Senator Mark Baisley

claims.text: The campaign's About page emphasizes her record as Secretary of State on election security and access: it says she led efforts to criminalize threats against election workers and tampering with voting equipment, implemented automatic voter registration, and increased secure drop boxes. It says she will defend the rights and freedoms of all Coloradans and that she urged removing President Trump from the ballot.

The campaign's About page says she was elected Colorado's 39th Secretary of State in 2018 and reelected in 2022, earlier directed the Colorado governor's Washington, D.C. office, practiced international anti-corruption law, and earned a law degree from the University of Pennsylvania.

The campaign's home page lists these priorities: public safety and victims (holding repeat offenders accountable and working with local law enforcement); cost of living and taxpayers (reviewing state spending and cutting waste); investigating corruption and fraud; consumer protection, especially against scams targeting older adults; defending Colorado's water rights; and challenging federal overreach when Colorado's interests are harmed.

The campaign's home page says he served eight years in the U.S. Navy, has worked in prosecution for more than 20 years including as a consumer protection prosecutor in the Kansas Attorney General's Office, and was elected District Attorney of the Fourth Judicial District (El Paso and Teller counties) in 2020 and re-elected in 2024.
